USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The United States should stay in the 90-day truce (March 1 deadline) and keep negotiating: hold tariffs in place, press for concrete Chinese purchase commitments and structural progress (forced tech transfer, IP, market access), and keep the suspended $200B List-3 escalation from 10% to 25% as credible leverage. Do not escalate now (that would break the truce and further spook already-fragile markets) and do not concede (China has yet to deliver verified commitments).

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat reading: the trade dispute itself is not an existential or even high threat to the US — the domestic economy is firm (IP index 104.09 and rising, CPI ~2% YoY, consumer sentiment 98.3, Fed funds 2.27% per country_health) and Washington holds the terrain with tariffs on $250B of imports in place while the $200B escalation is suspended as an incentive (event_timeline 2018-12-01 G20 deal; PBS/CNBC). The risks that keep this from being a strong opportunity are second-order: the Huawei/Meng arrest and China's detention of two Canadians (timeline 2018-12-01, 2018-12-10) could spiral and derail the truce; US equities sit at year lows with the 10Y yield sliding to ~2.77% and Baa spreads widening to ~5.04% (country_health) as markets weigh trade uncertainty plus Fed tightening; and Xi's mid-December speech offered no concrete proposals (NYT/CNBC). That reads as a modest net opportunity with genuine fragility. Action stance: with the truce only ~3 weeks old, engage in talks without new commitments — maximize leverage while the escalation lever is still live and the March 1 deadline concentrates Beijing, but avoid committing concessions before China demonstrates delivery, so the 25% escalation and broader tariff options remain the natural fallback if talks fail (Dorsey eligible outline). Escalation now forfeits leverage and amplifies market stress; full concession surrenders a strong position for unverified promises.
key_factors: 90-day truce with March 1 deadline; tariffs on $250B still in place and $200B 10%→25% escalation suspended as leverage
US macro firm: rising industrial production, ~2% CPI, 98.3 consumer sentiment — no material domestic GDP drag yet
Market fragility: S&P at 2018 lows, 10Y yield falling to ~2.77%, Baa spreads widening to ~5.04%, oil collapse — trade uncertainty + Fed tightening
Huawei CFO Meng arrest and Canada/China detentions create an escalatory overlay that could derail the truce
China's purchase/structural commitments remain vague with no verified delivery

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should hold the course within the 90-day G20 negotiation window and press for a durable settlement — cementing the suspension of the threatened January 1 tariff hike from 10% to 25% and defusing the Huawei/Meng Wanzhou crisis so it does not metastasize into full tech decoupling. Now is the time to negotiate seriously, not to escalate or to capitulate: escalation (e.g., further detention of foreigners) has already damaged our standing with a Western ally and risks reinstating the punished tariff schedule, while full concession on structural reform would undercut our tech-autonomy agenda and domestic credibility for little guaranteed return.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is high but not existential. The trade war is demonstrably biting: US Section 301 tariffs now cover roughly $250B of Chinese exports (final List 1/2 at 25% and List 3 at 10%, per timeline entries of 09-24 and 08-23), and China's November export growth collapsed to +5.4% y/y — the weakest since March — with imports +3%, the slowest since 2016, as front-loading faded. The growth picture is fragile (Q3 GDP 6.5%, slowest since 2009; Shanghai Composite down ~25% ytd; yuan down >5%, reserves being deployed to defend it). Most concerning is the firm-level/non-tariff escalation: Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Canada on a US extradition request tied to alleged Iran-sanctions violations on the very day of the truce, and Beijing's retaliatory detention of two Canadians (Kovrig, Spavor) has drawn diplomatic backlash — a genuine threat to our flagship tech champion and to CCP tech-self-sufficiency goals, squarely at the +0.5 anchor. Countering that, the 12-01 G20 outcome suspended the Jan 1 hike (tariffs remain at 10%) and both sides are in active negotiation, so the worst-case trajectory is paused — which keeps this below existential. On action: with a live truce and a credible risk that escalation (further hostage-taking, hard counter-tariffs) invites the 25% reinstatement and deeper decoupling, the disciplined move is to negotiate — use the window to secure the tariff freeze and a face-saving resolution of the Huawei matter, while balking at structural reforms that would dismantle Made in China 2025. That justifies a mildly de-escalatory hold at negotiate rather than escalation or unconditional concession.
